strengths: The paper identifies a practically meaningful gap: existing medical reasoning segmentation methods are single-round, while real clinical interaction is naturally multi-round and refers back to earlier segmentation results. The MEMR-Seg task is well motivated and clearly defined, with a plausible taxonomy of five inter-entity relationship types (organ-lesion, anatomical hierarchy, spatial, attribute, inferential).

MR-MedSeg is a substantial resource: 177K multi-round dialogues, 118K images, 569K masks, 168 entity categories, and 9 modalities, built with an explicit semi-automatic pipeline (entity selection, relationship generation, template integration, GPT-5 refinement, plus medical-expert filtering). The construction process is described in enough detail to be reproducible in spirit, and proper attribution is given to SA-Med2D-20M.

The baseline model (MediRound) is sensibly designed: extending SegLLM-style multi-round reasoning with medical backbones (LLaVA-Med + MedSAM), using cropped reference objects and bounding-box coordinates as cross-round reference features. The design choices are ablated (segmentation head, MLLM, LoRA vs. frozen).

The paper honestly identifies the train/test discrepancy induced by teacher forcing (GT masks at training vs. self-generated masks at inference) and proposes the lightweight JCM to mitigate error propagation. The ablations on the threshold β and per-round results (Table 2) support the claim that JCM helps more as the number of rounds increases.

Evaluation is fairly broad: human-assisted traditional segmentation pipelines, MLLM+segmentation-model hybrids, SegLLM, single-round referring segmentation (Table 3), qualitative comparisons, and component ablations. The reported gains (~15%) over the closest baselines are large.
weaknesses: Dialogue diversity is a real concern. The queries are generated from 50–80 templates per relationship type and then refined by GPT-5, so the 'reasoning' largely reduces to template-pattern matching (e.g., 'segment the other X of instance 1'). Because training and test data come from the same template distribution, the evaluation may overestimate generalization to free-form, natural clinical queries. No out-of-template or held-out-relationship evaluation is provided.

The reliability of the semi-automatic annotation is not quantified. Spatial and attribute relationships are claimed to be verified with image context and screened by three inspectors, but no statistics are given: how many relationships were checked, inter-annotator agreement, rejection rates, or estimated label error rates. Given that GPT-generated anatomical/spatial claims can be subtly wrong, the dataset's label quality remains largely unverified.

The JCM is under-specified. The supervision used to train the Quality Judgment Module (what defines a 'low-quality' [SEG] feature, and the label source) and the objective of the Correction Module are deferred to an appendix not included. Moreover, the β ablation (Figure 7) shows differences of only ~0.1–0.5 points across thresholds, which raises questions about how meaningful the judgment threshold is and about robustness; the mechanism's gains should also be disentangled from simply re-decoding features.

Baseline fairness and protocol clarity: the 'Human-Thinking' comparison protocol is described only informally, and the hybrid MLLM+segmentation pipelines may be handicapped by prompt-format mismatch rather than genuine capability gaps. Per-round numbers in Table 2 are also inconsistent with the hard/regular splits in Table 1 in ways that are not explained (e.g., some baselines improve sharply at later rounds).

Correctness of multi-round reasoning is only measured via mask-overlap metrics (Dice/gIoU/cIoU). There is no analysis of whether the model actually resolves the referring expression correctly versus coincidentally overlapping the target, and no error decomposition (wrong referent vs. poor mask). A user study or reasoning-correctness audit would substantially strengthen the claims.

Reproducibility and polish issues: the project URL in the abstract is truncated ('https://github.com/' with no repository), the Appendix containing key JCM training details and dataset statistics is not available for review, and reference [1] (cited as GPT-5) is actually the GPT-4 technical report.

The methodological novelty is limited: MediRound is a fairly direct medical-domain instantiation of SegLLM, and JCM is a small MLP-based test-time filter. The contribution therefore rests mostly on the dataset/task, which makes the missing data-quality quantification more consequential. No discussion of clinical/safety limitations of a possibly hallucinating medical dialogue system is provided.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically motivated gap: existing medical reasoning-segmentation methods are single-round, while realistic clinical interaction is inherently multi-round and refers back to earlier segmentation results. The MEMR-Seg task formulation is clear and the two required capabilities (cross-round entity reasoning, accurate mask generation) are well articulated.

The MR-MedSeg dataset is a substantial artifact: 177K multi-round dialogues, 118K images, 569K masks, 168 entity categories across 9 modalities, built on the public SA-Med2D-20M source with a documented three-step semi-automatic construction pipeline (entity selection, relationship generation, template integration) and human inspection.

MediRound is a reasonable and clearly described baseline: reference-round masks are used to crop and box-encode the referred entity, concatenated with full dialogue history into the MLLM input, extending SegLLM-style multi-round reasoning to the medical domain.

The evaluation is comparatively broad: multi-round and single-round benchmarks, per-round breakdowns (Table 2), a hybrid MLLM+segmenter paradigm, SegLLM transfers, and ablations over vision backbone, MLLM backbone, and JCM threshold.

The train/test discrepancy introduced by teacher forcing in multi-round settings is explicitly identified, and the inference-time Judgment & Correction Mechanism is a lightweight, training-free attempt to address error propagation.
weaknesses: The central evaluation fairness concern: the multi-round comparisons (Table 1/2) appear to pit MediRound, which is trained end-to-end on MR-MedSeg, against baselines (SegLLM, Human-Thinking + specialist models, MLLM+segmenter hybrids) that seemingly are not fine-tuned on the same dataset. Beating unadapted baselines on a benchmark you built largely shows distribution familiarity, not a superior method. A fine-tuned SegLLM or other multi-round-adapted baseline on MR-MedSeg is necessary to support the claim of 'surpassing conventional approaches.'

The dataset's 'reasoning' is largely template-driven: entity relationships are generated from five predefined scenario templates (50–80 paraphrases each) and refined by GPT-5. Cross-round 'reasoning' may reduce to memorizable template patterns tied to a fixed taxonomy of 168 entities, raising doubts about whether the benchmark measures genuine entity-level reasoning or template completion. No out-of-distribution or unseen-relationship evaluation is reported.

The Judgment & Correction Mechanism is weakly motivated and under-specified in the main paper. There is no analysis of what the Quality Judgment Module is actually measuring, how its supervision labels are defined (if derived from ground-truth mask quality, this risks information leakage concerns that must be clarified), or why a shallow MLP correction in [SEG] feature space should repair a semantically wrong prediction. Gains from JCM are modest overall (e.g., Dice 55.8→58.4) and the β ablation differences are within ~0.5–1 point, which is within plausible noise; no variance or significance testing is provided anywhere in the paper.

The single-round results undercut the 'effective baseline' claim: on Table 3, MediRound loses to MediSee on gIoU (48.3 vs 50.4) and cIoU (66.3 vs 70.8), and the ablation shows MedSAM without LoRA already achieves the reported numbers, suggesting the multi-round machinery contributes little to standard referring segmentation.

Per-round results contain anomalies that are not discussed: e.g., Table 2 shows performance generally increasing with round number for MediRound (50.2 → 64.7 by Round 7), which contradicts the paper's own error-accumulation narrative, and the Round 8 jump for JCM (46.1 → 54.8) is unexplained. Figure 7 (β ablation) is cluttered to the point of being illegible.

Citation hygiene is poor and undermines trust: GPT-5 is cited to the GPT-4 technical report [1], Qwen3-VL is cited to the 2023 Qwen report [3], Gemini-2.5-Pro to the original Gemini report [38], and the project link is a truncated 'https://github.com/' placeholder, weakening reproducibility claims.

Missing details hamper reproducibility and scrutiny: the definition of 'regular case' vs 'hard case', the exact protocol of the 'Human-Thinking' baselines (who the humans were, how queries were decomposed, inter-annotator agreement), the role of the 'READ' [30] addition, and JCM training specifics are all deferred to an appendix not provided here. No statistical significance, no per-modality breakdown, and no clinical or expert evaluation of the dialogue quality or generated masks.

There is no limitations or societal-impact discussion despite the medical domain; the safety implications of deploying an interactive medical segmentation assistant (and the risk of plausible-but-wrong masks in later dialogue rounds) are not acknowledged.

Scope appropriateness: the contribution is best characterized as Datasets/Benchmarks plus a Concept & Feasibility baseline rather than an algorithmic advance; judged under that lens, the dataset's template-driven nature and the unfair baseline comparison are more consequential, since the benchmark itself is the main contribution and its validity is the key open question.

strengths: Well-motivated new task: the paper identifies a genuine and practically relevant gap — existing medical reasoning segmentation methods (LISA-style, MedSeg-R, MediSee, etc.) are single-round, while real clinical workflows involve iterative, entity-referential queries. Defining MEMR-Seg is a meaningful conceptual contribution.

Substantial dataset contribution: MR-MedSeg (177K multi-round dialogues, 118K images, 569K masks, 168 entity categories, 9 modalities) is, to my knowledge, the first large-scale multi-round medical reasoning segmentation dataset, with a documented semi-automatic construction pipeline (entity selection, relationship generation, template integration, GPT-based refinement, plus three medical inspectors for filtering).

Reasonable baseline design: MediRound extends SegLLM-style multi-round segmentation to the medical domain by injecting reference-round crops, bounding-box embeddings, and conversational history into the MLLM input. The architecture is clearly described and sensible.

The train/test discrepancy created by teacher forcing on ground-truth references is an honest and important limitation to identify, and the proposed inference-time Judgment & Correction Mechanism is a lightweight (two-MLP) and computationally cheap mitigation with clearly positive results, particularly in later rounds (Table 2), which is consistent with the error-accumulation hypothesis.

Comparatively thorough experiments: baselines include specialist models with human re-prompting, MLLM+segmenter hybrid pipelines, SegLLM adapted to the domain, per-round breakdowns (Table 2), single-round evaluation on SA-Med2D-20M (Table 3), and ablations on backbone choices and the JCM threshold β. The backbone ablations (SAM vs. MedSAM, LLaVA vs. LLaVA-Med) support the design choices.
Reproducibility signals are reasonably good: implementation details (hardware, LoRA rank, LR, scheduler, JCM MLP dimensions), pseudocode for the JCM inference procedure, and a stated project release.
weaknesses: Dataset linguistic diversity is a concern: dialogues are ultimately generated from 50–80 templates per relationship type with entities inserted, refined by GPT-5. This raises the risk that MR-MedSeg rewards template-pattern matching rather than genuine multi-round entity reasoning. The paper would be stronger with held-out template variants, paraphrase stress tests, or an analysis of how performance degrades on out-of-template phrasing; this is not addressed.

The data quality control is described only at a high level. How many dialogues did the three medical inspectors actually screen, what were the rejection rates and inter-annotator agreement? Given the heavy reliance on GPT-5 for relationships and refinement, quantitative validation of relationship correctness (especially image-dependent spatial relationships) is needed; currently this is deferred to the appendix.

The JCM training objective is underspecified in the main text. How is the 'quality' label for the Quality Judgment Module defined (e.g., thresholded Dice against GT of the current round)? If quality labels are derived from ground-truth masks, JCM partially leaks GT information at inference time, which would need clarification. The correction MLP refining a 256-d [SEG] feature also seems underpowered relative to the reported gains (+2.6 Dice overall, +8.7 cIoU at Round #8); more analysis of where the improvement comes from would help.

Evaluation on own benchmark only: all multi-round results are on MR-MedSeg, which the authors also trained on. There is no cross-dataset or out-of-distribution generalization test (e.g., multi-round dialogues built over a different medical source), so the claim of general multi-round medical reasoning capability is weakly supported.

Some baseline comparisons feel contrived: 'Human-Thinking + model' rows require expert annotators in the loop per query, which is expensive and hard to standardize/reproduce; the paper does not report how many humans, their protocol consistency, or variance. Also, minor table anomalies (e.g., SegLLM-7B gIoU 42.4 exceeding its Dice 42.1 in the 'regular case' column while overall gIoU 27.5 is far below Dice 36.3) suggest a possible reporting inconsistency worth double-checking.

The comparison with GPT-4o/Gemini-2.5-Pro/Qwen3-VL hybrid pipelines uses zero-shot MLLM prompting without fine-tuning on multi-round data, which limits the strength of the 'end-to-end training is better' claim; a fine-tuned smaller MLLM in the hybrid paradigm would be a fairer control.

No significance testing or variance reporting across the large result tables; given ~1.2K test conversations, several of the smaller differences (e.g., MediRound vs. MediRound+READ) may not be statistically meaningful.

Minor clarity issues: the GitHub link in the abstract is incomplete; notation in Eq. (1) mixes encoders loosely (x_crop and x_box are described but the crop extraction procedure depends on GT masks at training time, which should be stated explicitly up front); Figure 7 is dense and hard to read. No discussion of societal/clinical-safety implications despite the medical setting (e.g., risk of propagated errors in clinical use), which the authors are well positioned to add given their own error-propagation analysis.

strengths: The paper introduces a clearly defined new task (MEMR-Seg) that addresses a genuine gap: existing medical reasoning segmentation approaches are single-round, while multi-round reasoning segmentation has only been explored in natural images (SegLLM). The motivation via realistic clinical interaction patterns is convincing.

The MR-MedSeg dataset is a substantial resource: 177K multi-round dialogues, 118K images, 569K masks, 168 entity categories, and 9 imaging modalities. The construction pipeline is well documented (entity selection from SA-Med2D-20M, semi-automatic relationship generation, template integration with GPT-5 refinement, and review by three medically trained inspectors), with useful per-scenario statistics and analyses (Appendix D) supporting transparency.

The baseline model (MediRound) is sensibly designed, combining MedSAM, LLaVA-Med, reference-mask cropping, bounding-box encoding, and conversation history, with a clear formulation and pseudocode. The Judgment & Correction Mechanism (JCM) is a lightweight, well-motivated response to the error-propagation problem inherent to chain-like multi-round pipelines, and its gains grow with round count as expected (Table 2).

Experimental evaluation is reasonably thorough: comparisons against human-assisted traditional segmenters, MLLM+segmenter hybrid paradigms, and an adapted SegLLM; evaluation on both the new multi-round benchmark and a vanilla referring segmentation benchmark (SA-Med2D-20M); and ablations covering segmentation/MLLM backbones, the JCM threshold, and reference-information strategies. Metrics (Dice, gIoU, cIoU) and regular/hard case splits are appropriate.

The limitations section is candid and substantive (single-entity rounds, long-sequence fragility, loss of general conversational ability, 2D-only restriction), and the contribution type (dataset/benchmark plus baseline) is appropriate for a venue like ECCV.
weaknesses: Dataset diversity and reasoning depth are a concern: dialogues are built from 50-80 'semantically equivalent' templates per relationship type, so linguistic and reasoning variability may be limited, and several scenarios (e.g., 'segment the other X', hierarchical sub-structure queries) reduce to relatively simple referential or spatial reasoning rather than deep clinical reasoning. The paper does not quantify template coverage or dialogue diversity beyond a word cloud and long-tail frequency plot.

All evaluation is on the authors' own benchmark built from the same pipeline as training data, with no external or cross-dataset test set. This raises concerns about self-favoring evaluation and about how well results transfer; the small validation/test splits (1,270/1,273 conversations) and severe scenario imbalance (e.g., only 2 max rounds for Spatial Relationship) further limit the robustness of conclusions.

Several methodological details and fairness issues are underexplored: (i) the train/test discrepancy from teacher forcing with ground-truth reference masks is acknowledged but the JCM's reliance on ground-truth IoU as a quality target during its training (Appendix A.2) could be a shortcut that does not generalize; (ii) the adaptation protocols for SegLLM and hybrid baselines are not described in detail, making fairness of comparisons hard to verify; (iii) the β ablation differences are marginal (e.g., 52.4-52.6 overall), so the claimed sensitivity analysis is weak evidence.

There are presentation and reproducibility gaps: the project URL in the abstract is incomplete; data/model release is only promised 'in the final submission version'; per-round Table 2 shows cIoU only and mixes an incomplete-round structure; some baseline rows in Table 1 (e.g., SegLLM-13B with unusually high gIoU on regular cases) invite scrutiny. GPT-5-generated data also raises attribution/verification questions that would benefit from a released annotation audit.

Several strong claims lack supporting analysis: the 'approximately 15% improvement' is stated loosely without confidence intervals or statistical testing; qualitative examples (Figures 6, C) are cherry-picked without failure-case analysis; and the JCM's improvement mechanism is asserted rather than dissected (e.g., no analysis of what fraction of [SEG] features are judged low-quality or how corrections change masks).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and practically relevant gap: existing medical reasoning segmentation methods are single-round, while real clinical interaction is iterative and refers back to earlier mask outputs. Formalizing the MEMR-Seg task is a reasonable framing.

The MR-MedSeg dataset is a substantial resource effort: 177K multi-round dialogues, 118K images, 569K masks, 168 entity categories, and 9 modalities built on top of SA-Med2D-20M, with a documented three-stage construction pipeline and human inspection by medically trained reviewers.

The evaluation is fairly broad for a new task: multiple baseline families (human-assisted specialist models, MLLM+segmenter hybrids, SegLLM adapted to the medical domain), per-round breakdowns, single-round referring segmentation results, and ablations on backbones, reference-mask extraction strategies, and the JCM threshold.

The Judgment & Correction Mechanism is lightweight (two small MLPs) and targets a real problem (error propagation in chain-like multi-round inference); the per-round results in Table 2 plausibly support its benefit. The limitations section (Appendix F) is candid about single-object outputs, long-sequence fragility, catastrophic loss of conversational ability, and 2D-only processing.
weaknesses: The 'reasoning' in the dataset is largely templated rather than emergent. Appendix D.1 reveals that references to prior rounds follow a small set of fixed phrasings ('referring to the output of round N', 'instance N', 'its ...'), and Step 3 generates 50-80 semantically equivalent templates per relationship. This creates a serious shortcut-learning risk: the model may solve the task by pattern-matching template structure and index tokens rather than performing entity-level reasoning. The paper provides no probe or out-of-template evaluation to rule this out, which undermines the central claim.

The core technical contribution is thin. MediRound is essentially SegLLM's architecture re-implemented with LLaVA-Med + MedSAM, and the JCM is a small post-hoc MLP head. The perceived 15-point improvement largely reflects training on in-domain data rather than a novel mechanism.

The JCM has a circularity problem: both the Quality Judgment and Correction modules are trained using ground-truth masks (ground-truth IoU as the soft quality target, and mask loss for correction) on the same distribution, then applied only at test time. It is unclear why a learned IoU predictor on frozen features plus a one-shot MLP correction generalizes better than simply decoding again, and no analysis of when judgment fails is given.

Evaluation is confined to the authors' own test split of their own dataset (only 1,273 test conversations, with scenario-level imbalance, e.g., only 151 conversations for two of five scenario types). There is no external benchmark or held-out dataset to assess generalization of either the dataset design or the model, and cross-dataset evaluation (e.g., MedSeg-R or MedDr datasets) is absent.

Baseline fairness is questionable. SegLLM was designed and trained for natural images; reporting its low medical performance as evidence of MediRound's superiority conflates domain adaptation with the proposed mechanism. The 'Human-Thinking' baselines are described only vaguely, and it is unclear how human reasoning was standardized, costed, or validated across the three inspector annotators.

The dataset inherits SA-Med2D-20M's known mask-noise issues without quantifying annotation quality; and the automated GPT-5 refinement + template pipeline raises reproducibility concerns, although release is promised only 'in the final submission version' rather than being available at review time.

Presentation issues reduce confidence: Table 1's val vs. test column grouping is confusing; the paper cites the GPT-4 technical report for 'GPT-5'; the GitHub link in the abstract is incomplete; and claims like 'encompasses nearly all multi-round interaction scenarios encountered in real-world medical applications' are overclaimed given the five fixed template families.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated new task definition (MEMR-Seg): multi-round, entity-level reasoning segmentation in medical images is a natural and practically relevant extension of single-round reasoning segmentation (LISA, MedSeg-R, MediSee) and multi-round segmentation in natural images (SegLLM), and the gap in the medical domain is convincingly argued.

Substantial dataset contribution: MR-MedSeg (177K multi-round conversations, 118K images, 569K masks, 168 entity categories, 9 modalities) built on the public SA-Med2D-20M source, with a documented three-stage construction pipeline, five well-defined interaction scenarios, and medical-expert screening. This is the core value of the paper as a Datasets/Benchmarks-style contribution.

Comprehensive experimental protocol: the paper compares against human-assisted specialist models, hybrid MLLM+segmenter pipelines (GPT-4o/Gemini/Qwen3-VL paired with IMIS-Net/MediSee), SegLLM adapted to the medical domain, and reports per-round breakdowns (Table 2) that directly illustrate error accumulation in chain-like multi-round segmentation.

The Judgment & Correction Mechanism is a sensible, lightweight response to the train/test discrepancy induced by teacher forcing in multi-round segmentation, and the ablations (backbone choices, beta threshold, reference-information extraction in Appendix C) support the design decisions.

Honest limitations section (single entity per round, long-sequence fragility, loss of conversational ability, 2D-only) and promised release of data and code support reproducibility and follow-up work.
weaknesses: The 'reasoning' in the dataset is largely template-driven. Dialogues are generated by filling 50-80 GPT-5-produced templates with entity relationships, and cross-round references follow three fixed phrasing strategies (Appendix D.1). This raises the question of how much genuine entity-level reasoning is required versus pattern matching over a small set of syntactic reference patterns; the benchmark may overestimate reasoning capability and could be gameable by the model's own training distribution.

Methodological novelty is limited: MediRound is essentially SegLLM's design transplanted to the medical domain with LLaVA-Med + MedSAM and LoRA. The strongest single-round result (Table 3) is only on par with MediSee (Dice 62.1 vs 61.2, but lower gIoU), so the method's advantage rests almost entirely on the new benchmark it introduces, which creates a self-referential evaluation concern.

Some baseline comparisons appear uneven or strawman-like: 'Human-Thinking + X' protocols are not precisely specified (how many humans, protocol, inter-annotator agreement, cost), and comparisons such as Grounding DINO + SAM-Med2D/MedSAM are known-weak for this task. Statistical significance is not reported, and validation/test sets per scenario are small (e.g., 98-374 images in some validation scenarios), so per-round differences may be noisy.

The JCM ablation on beta (Figure 7) shows very small differences (52.4-52.6 overall), which weakens the claim that the mechanism's threshold is meaningful; moreover, JCM's quality-judgment ground truth is derived from IoU against ground-truth masks during training, so the mechanism benefits from supervision unavailable to the compared baselines.

The train/test discrepancy from teacher forcing is acknowledged but not actually addressed during training (e.g., scheduled sampling or self-generated reference masks are not explored), leaving the model dependent on an inference-time patch; a direct comparison against exposure-bias mitigation at training time would strengthen the case for JCM.

Dataset quality validation is thin: the paper states three medical inspectors filtered the data, but provides no quantitative quality metrics, agreement rates, or error estimates for the GPT-5-generated relationships and templates; potential factual errors in GPT-5-produced anatomical/attribute relationships are not quantified.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in the submission: the GitHub URL is truncated/empty, release of data and code is promised only 'in the final submission version', and key hyperparameters (loss weights lambda_bce, lambda_dice, JCM training data construction) are deferred or unspecified.
